content: The primary goal in managing epilepsy is to achieve remission, defined as a period of seizure freedom, through the use of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) and subsequently discontinue these medications without triggering a recurrence of seizures. Prolonged use of AEDs is associated with potential long-term adverse effects, making it reasonable to consider discontinuing the medication once remission is achieved. However, the timing and method of withdrawal—whether rapid or slow—are critical factors to consider when discontinuing AEDs. This review evaluates the evidence regarding the rate of AED withdrawal and its impact on seizure recurrence. It is an updated version of a Cochrane Review initially published in 2020. The objective of this review is to quantify the risk of seizure recurrence following either rapid withdrawal (defined as a tapering period of three months or less) or slow withdrawal (defined as a tapering period of more than three months) of AEDs in adults and children with epilepsy who are in remission. Additionally, the review aims to identify variables that may influence the risk of seizure recurrence. For the most recent update, conducted on November 8, 2021, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE (Ovid), and SCOPUS. The search included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials from sources such as PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and the Cochrane Review Groups' Specialized Registers. No language restrictions were applied. The review included randomized controlled trials that assessed the withdrawal of AEDs using either a rapid or slow tapering approach after varying durations of seizure control in individuals with epilepsy. Two independent reviewers evaluated the trials for inclusion and extracted relevant data. The outcomes assessed included seizure freedom at one, two, and five years following AED withdrawal, time to seizure recurrence, occurrence of status epilepticus, mortality, seizure-related morbidity (e.g., injuries, fractures, aspiration pneumonia), and quality of life as measured by validated scales. Two studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. The first study involved 57 children with epilepsy who had been seizure-free for at least two years. Participants were randomized to taper their AEDs over one month or six months. This study was not blinded, and details regarding the randomization process were not provided. Over a follow-up period of 54 months, 20 out of 30 participants in the one-month tapering group remained seizure-free, compared to 15 out of 27 participants in the six-month tapering group. However, there was no statistically significant difference between the groups, and no data were available to compare the timing of seizure recurrence between the two groups. The second study included 149 children and showed a non-significant trend toward a lower risk of seizure recurrence one year after AED withdrawal in the slow tapering group (risk ratio [RR] 0.76, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.58 to 1.01; P = 0.06; very low-certainty evidence). At the two-year mark, 30 participants in the rapid tapering group and 29 participants in the slow tapering group remained seizure-free (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.29; P = 0.48; very low-certainty evidence). At five years, 10 participants in the rapid tapering group and six participants in the slow tapering group were seizure-free (RR 1.40, 95% CI 0.54 to 3.65; P = 0.49; very low-certainty evidence). No data were available for other outcomes, such as status epilepticus, mortality, or quality of life. Due to methodological differences and variations in tapering duration between the two studies, a quantitative synthesis of the results was not performed. Additionally, an ongoing Italian trial is investigating whether the rate of AED withdrawal (rapid or slow) affects seizure relapse in adults with focal or generalized epilepsy who have been seizure-free for at least two years. No preliminary results from this trial are currently available. The authors concluded that, due to methodological limitations and the small sample sizes of the included studies, no reliable conclusions can be drawn regarding the optimal rate of AED tapering. Using the GRADE approach, the certainty of the evidence was assessed as very low for all reported outcomes. Both studies were judged to have a high risk of bias. Further research is needed in both adults and children to determine the optimal rate of AED withdrawal and to explore the influence of factors such as seizure type, underlying etiology, intellectual disability, electroencephalographic abnormalities, neurological deficits, and other comorbidities on the withdrawal process.
